o: Every element appears three times except one element appearing once and one appearing twice; recover both in O(n) time and O(1) space. Example 1: [2,2,3,2,5,5,5,7,7] → once = 3, twice = 7. Bit counting per bit position works because counts modulo 3 reveal which elements contributed 1 or 2 copies of each bit.
k: Per bit, total count mod 3 is 1 for bits of the unique-once element and 2 for bits of the twice element.
The classic two-variable trick (ones ^= x & ~twos; twos ^= x & ~ones) keeps a ternary counter per bit in two words, separating 'seen once' from 'seen twice'.

a.i: Maintain `ones` (bits seen 1 mod 3 times) and `twos` (bits seen 2 mod 3 times). Each number updates both with masking so a bit cycles 00 → 10 (ones) → 01 (twos) → 00. After processing, elements appearing three times leave no trace, the once element sits in `ones`, the twice element in `twos`. Works for negative numbers since XOR/masks operate on the raw two's-complement representation.
s: For each x: ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work per element.

a.i: For each of the 32 bit positions, sum that bit over all numbers. count % 3 == 1 marks a bit of the once element; count % 3 == 2 marks a bit of the twice element. Reassemble both results, converting the sign bit correctly for negatives.
s: For b in 0..31, count numbers with bit b set.
If count % 3 == 1 set bit b of `once`; if == 2 set bit b of `twice`.
a.t: O(32n) — constant number of passes over the array.

w: Lead with the two-variable trick — it is the expected O(n)/O(1) answer; fall back to bit counting if asked to explain the invariant intuitively. Pitfalls: mixing up which variable holds the once vs twice element, and sign handling in JavaScript/Python when reconstructing from bits. Follow-up: generalize to 'one element appears k times, rest appear m times'.
